subject: Economics
description: Covers 1969 Nationalization, RBI formation, SBI history, and Narasimham Committee.

questions.stem: In which year did the Government of India nationalize 14 major private commercial banks to align the banking sector with the socialist goals of the state?
questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: On July 19, 1969, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi announced the nationalization of 14 major commercial banks (those with deposits of over Rs 50 crore). The objective was to force banks to expand into rural areas and provide credit to agriculture and small-scale industries (Priority Sector Lending), rather than just lending to large urban industrialists who often owned these banks.
DECOY BUSTING: A second wave of nationalization occurred in 1980, when 6 more banks were nationalized. 1955 was the year the Imperial Bank of India was nationalized to form SBI. 1991 marked the LPG reforms (liberalization), which eventually allowed private banks back in.
EXAM INSIGHT: Bank nationalization is considered one of the most defining economic decisions in modern Indian history. It massively expanded the bank branch network into unbanked rural areas, though it later led to issues with efficiency and Non-Performing Assets (NPAs).

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established on April 1, 1935, based on the recommendations of which commission?

options.option_text: Hilton Young Commission
Simon Commission
Hunter Commission
Sarkaria Commission

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The RBI was established following the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, popularly known as the Hilton Young Commission (submitted its report in 1926). The RBI Act was passed in 1934, and operations began in 1935.
DECOY BUSTING: The Simon Commission (1927) was for constitutional reforms. The Hunter Commission (1919) investigated the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) reviewed Centre-State relations.
EXAM INSIGHT: RBI was initially set up as a private shareholders' bank with its central office in Calcutta. It was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937. It was nationalized immediately after independence in 1949.

questions.stem: Which historical bank was nationalized in 1955 to create the State Bank of India (SBI)?

options.option_text: Imperial Bank of India
Bank of Bengal
Oudh Commercial Bank
Punjab National Bank

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Imperial Bank of India was formed in 1921 by merging three presidency banks (Bank of Bengal, Bank of Bombay, and Bank of Madras). Before the RBI was established, the Imperial Bank acted as a quasi-central bank. In 1955, following the Gorwala Committee recommendations, the Imperial Bank was nationalized and renamed the State Bank of India to spearhead rural credit expansion.
DECOY BUSTING: Bank of Bengal was one of the three banks that merged to form the Imperial Bank. Oudh Commercial Bank (1881) was the first bank with limited liability managed by Indians. Punjab National Bank (1894) was the first bank wholly managed by Indians (Lala Lajpat Rai was a founder).
EXAM INSIGHT: SBI is not technically governed by the Banking Regulation Act like other banks; it is governed by a special statute, the State Bank of India Act, 1955. It remains India's largest public sector bank.

questions.stem: Who was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?

options.option_text: C. D. Deshmukh
Osborne Smith
Benegal Rama Rau
Manmohan Singh

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Chintaman Dwarkanath (C.D.) Deshmukh was the first Indian to be appointed as the Governor of the RBI. He served from 1943 to 1949. He oversaw the critical transition of the RBI from a colonial institution to a nationalized central bank for independent India.
DECOY BUSTING: Sir Osborne Smith was the very first Governor of the RBI (1935-1937), but he was British. Sir Benegal Rama Rau was the second Indian Governor (and the longest-serving one). Dr. Manmohan Singh served as RBI Governor much later (1982-1985).
EXAM INSIGHT: Deshmukh was a brilliant civil servant. He later served as India's Finance Minister. He famously resigned from Nehru's cabinet protesting the government's proposal to make Bombay a union territory during the linguistic reorganization of states.

questions.stem: In 1991, following the balance of payments crisis, which committee was set up to recommend comprehensive reforms for the Indian banking sector, leading to the entry of new private sector banks (like HDFC, ICICI)?

options.option_text: Narasimham Committee
Kelkar Committee
Rangarajan Committee
Urjit Patel Committee

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991), headed by former RBI Governor M. Narasimham, is the cornerstone of modern Indian banking reforms. It recommended lowering the SLR and CRR, deregulating interest rates, introducing prudential norms (capital adequacy, NPA classification), and granting licenses to new private sector banks (which broke the monopoly of public sector banks).
DECOY BUSTING: Kelkar Committee is famous for tax reforms (and later PPP models). Rangarajan Committee dealt with poverty estimation and disinvestment. Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended the shift to inflation targeting and the MPC framework.
EXAM INSIGHT: The licensing of new private banks in the 1990s (Generation 1 private banks) completely revolutionized retail banking in India, introducing ATMs, core banking software, and customer-centric services that forced PSU banks to modernize.

questions.stem: Which institution is regarded as the first bank to be established in India, predating all three Presidency Banks?

options.option_text: Bank of Bengal, established in 1806 in Calcutta under a British royal charter
Bank of Hindustan, founded in 1770 in Calcutta by agency house Alexander & Co.
Allahabad Bank, established in 1865 and known as India's oldest joint-stock bank
Presidency Bank of Bombay, set up in 1840 under a British government charter

questions.explanation: Bank of Hindustan (1770), set up by the Calcutta agency house Alexander & Co., is considered India's first bank; it wound up in 1832. Bank of Bengal (1806) is the most common wrong answer because it is the first Presidency Bank and a forerunner of the modern banking system, but it was established 36 years later than Bank of Hindustan.

questions.stem: During the second wave of bank nationalisation in 1980, how many private commercial banks were taken over, and which government carried out this action?

options.option_text: Four banks were taken over in 1980 under Charan Singh's coalition government
Five banks were taken over in 1980 under Morarji Desai's Janata Party government
Six banks were taken over in 1980 under Indira Gandhi's returning Congress government
Eight banks were taken over in 1980 under Indira Gandhi's sixth general election mandate

questions.explanation: In April 1980, the Indira Gandhi-led Congress government nationalised six more commercial banks — Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, and Vijaya Bank — raising the total to 20 nationalised banks. Options A and B are wrong on both the number and the ruling government; option D inflates the count to eight.

questions.stem: Prathama Bank, India's first Regional Rural Bank, was inaugurated on 2 October 1975 in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh. Which commercial bank sponsored its establishment?

options.option_text: State Bank of India, the largest public sector bank in the country
Punjab National Bank, a leading nationalised bank headquartered in New Delhi
Syndicate Bank, a Mangalore-based bank later merged into Canara Bank in 2020
Bank of Baroda, a major nationalised bank headquartered in Vadodara, Gujarat

questions.explanation: Syndicate Bank sponsored Prathama Bank under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976. Punjab National Bank is the most tempting distractor because Moradabad lies in North India — PNB's traditional heartland — but the actual sponsor was Syndicate Bank. Prathama Bank continues to operate today under Canara Bank's sponsorship following the 2020 merger.

questions.stem: NABARD was established in July 1982 as the apex institution for rural credit in India. Which committee's report directly led to its creation?

options.option_text: M. Narasimham Committee, which reviewed India's entire financial sector in 1991
B. Sivaraman Committee (CRAFICARD), which reviewed rural credit institutions
Gadgil Study Group, which devised the Lead Bank Scheme framework in 1969
R.N. Malhotra Committee, which reviewed India's insurance sector in the 1990s

questions.explanation: NABARD was set up following the recommendations of the B. Sivaraman Committee (formally the Committee to Review Arrangements for Institutional Credit for Agriculture and Rural Development — CRAFICARD, 1979–81). The Narasimham Committee (1991) addressed broader financial-sector liberalisation and is the most popular wrong answer; the Gadgil Study Group concerns the Lead Bank Scheme, not NABARD.

questions.stem: RBI launched the Lead Bank Scheme in December 1969, assigning each district to one designated commercial bank for credit planning. Whose report primarily formed the basis of this scheme?

options.option_text: S. Chakravarty Committee, which reviewed India's monetary system in 1985
F.K.F. Nariman Committee, which studied branch expansion and district-level banking
M. Narasimham Committee, which recommended sweeping financial sector reforms in 1991
K.S. Krishnaswamy Committee, which was constituted to define priority sector credit

questions.explanation: The Lead Bank Scheme was primarily based on the F.K.F. Nariman Committee report (1969), which recommended that each district be 'adopted' by a commercial bank to coordinate credit planning and branch expansion. The Gadgil Study Group (1969) also contributed conceptually, but the Nariman Committee is the standard credited source. The Narasimham Committee (1991) is completely unrelated to this scheme.

questions.stem: The Deposit Insurance Corporation (DIC), which later merged into DICGC in 1978, commenced operations on 1 January 1962. What was the initial deposit insurance ceiling per depositor per bank?

options.option_text: ₹500 per depositor, covering only savings and current account balances
₹1,500 per depositor, covering savings, fixed, and recurring deposit accounts
₹5,000 per depositor, a limit that was revised downward in later amendments
₹10,000 per depositor, benchmarked against international deposit insurance norms

questions.explanation: When DIC commenced under the Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, 1961, the insured limit was ₹1,500 per depositor per bank. It was progressively raised: ₹5,000 (1968), ₹10,000 (1970), ₹30,000 (1980), ₹1 lakh (1993), and ₹5 lakh (2020, post-YES Bank crisis). Option A (₹500) confuses an earlier draft proposal that was not adopted; option C falsely implies a downward revision.

questions.stem: The 1993 amalgamation of New Bank of India with Punjab National Bank was the only instance of a forced merger between two nationalised banks in post-independence India. What primarily triggered this unprecedented action?

options.option_text: RBI's directive to consolidate all public-sector banks in northern India under one entity
New Bank of India turned financially insolvent due to massive NPAs and large-scale fraud
Government's plan to reduce the total number of public sector banks to below fifteen
New Bank of India's capital adequacy breached the Basel I international minimum floor

questions.explanation: New Bank of India was declared financially unviable by RBI in 1992 owing to large non-performing assets accumulated through fraudulent lending, particularly in real estate. Under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, it was compulsorily merged with Punjab National Bank in 1993. Option D is the most tempting distractor because capital adequacy was a visible symptom, but the root cause was fraud-driven insolvency — not a Basel threshold breach per se.
